We’re supposed to be at 70%, but after a few families moved, we’re closer to 62%. If I use last season’s roster, we qualify, and the lower fee would keep dues affordable for all the kids. The department rarely audits rosters unless there’s a complaint. Should I submit the older numbers or report the current percentage even if it may raise costs?

I’m a shift lead at a grocery store, and last weekend two coworkers and I stayed late to finish a big inventory count. We forgot to clock out, and the system automatically recorded us as working until midnight, about two extra paid hours each. My manager is swamped and probably won’t notice unless I bring it up. Everyone on the team is tired of unpaid “favor” work and says we deserve it anyway. Payroll closes tomorrow, and correcting it would mean less money for all three of us. Should I tell my boss what happened or let it go?

I’m applying for a city parking permit, and the form asks whether my car is primarily kept at my apartment address. Technically it’s parked most nights at my girlfriend’s place outside the zone, but I still pay rent here and need the permit for my job downtown. If I answer strictly, I probably won’t qualify, and I’ll spend a lot more on parking. A neighbor told me the office never checks unless someone complains. I’m tempted to just list my apartment as the main location. What should I do?

My department missed a deadline on a grant report because I didn’t send the final receipts to finance in time. The university office emailed my boss asking whether the delay was due to a vendor issue, which would give us an automatic extension and avoid a warning on our file. One of the vendors did send a confusing invoice, but that wasn’t really the reason we were late. If I explain the whole thing, my mistake may reflect badly on our team. Should I let my boss use the vendor explanation or clarify what actually happened?

I work at a small marketing agency, and my boss asked me to update our internal skills spreadsheet before she assigns people to a new client project. I’m intermediate with a design tool, not advanced, but if I mark myself as advanced, my team is more likely to get the project and the bonus pool that comes with it. My coworkers say everyone exaggerates a little on these forms and we can figure it out as we go. The client won’t see the spreadsheet directly, but management will rely on it. Should I rate myself higher or be precise?

I’m organizing travel reimbursements for a student club conference. The university reimburses meals only if we submit itemized receipts, but two members lost theirs and only have credit card charges showing the restaurant totals. If I submit a summary and say the itemized receipts were provided at check-in, the finance office may approve the full reimbursement, which would help our club budget and keep the students from paying out of pocket. If I’m transparent, the claim may be denied. I’m the treasurer and have to send it today. What should I do?

I’m a shift lead at a small café, and last week two of my coworkers forgot to log a few food waste items before closing. Our manager is reviewing inventory because costs are up, and she asked me directly whether anything unusual happened on my shifts. If I mention the missed logs, the team could lose our monthly bonus and my coworkers might get written up. If I just say closing was normal, nobody will probably trace it back to us. I like my team and know it was an honest mistake, but I’m also responsible for the closing records. What should I do?

I’m applying for a city parking permit that would make my commute much cheaper. The form asks whether I primarily live at my aunt’s address, which is inside the permit zone. I stay there one or two nights a week to help her after surgery, but my actual apartment is outside the zone. My aunt says I can use her address because I do spend time there, and lots of people bend these rules. If I don’t, I’ll keep paying a lot for parking near work. Should I list her address and leave out the details, or explain the situation?

I work in a lab at my university, and our department is being audited for equipment usage. My professor asked everyone to submit hours for a shared machine. A few of us used it for a student side project that wasn’t technically approved under the grant, but the results helped our class and didn’t damage anything. If I report the hours accurately, it could create trouble for my professor and the students involved. If I categorize them under routine training, the audit will probably pass smoothly. I’m not sure how transparent I need to be with the university office. What should I do?

My boss asked me to prepare a client status report for a software rollout. We’re mostly on track, but my teammate and I missed one internal security checklist step that we can still complete before launch. If I mention it now, our manager may escalate it and cancel the team’s Friday demo, which everyone has worked hard for. If I write that all internal checks are progressing as scheduled and fix the checklist tomorrow, the client and leadership likely won’t know. I don’t want to make the team look careless over something fixable. How should I handle the report?

I’m the treasurer for a community sports league, and we’re applying for a small grant from the parks department. The application asks whether we have any unpaid facility fees. We do have an overdue balance from last season, but the league president says we plan to pay it after registration money comes in, and disclosing it may disqualify us. The grant would pay for new equipment that all the kids need, especially families who can’t afford extra fees. I’m the one submitting the application online. Should I leave that part blank, answer no, or explain the overdue balance?

I’m a junior analyst at a small marketing firm, and my team missed a client reporting deadline because we spent two days fixing a mistake our manager made in the data pull. The client doesn’t know any of this yet, and my boss asked me to send the update saying the delay was due to “unexpected system issues.” If I refuse, the team may look disorganized and we could lose the account, which might affect bonuses. If I go along, I’d be misleading the client to protect us and my boss. What should I do?

I work at a city recreation center, and we’re applying for a grant that funds after-school programs. The application asks how many students attended regularly last semester. Our actual regular attendance was lower than expected, but if we count kids who came once or twice, we meet the threshold. My supervisor suggested using the broader number because the grant would keep two staff members employed and help us run summer programs. I’d be the one entering the figure in the official form. Should I use the number my supervisor wants, or flag the difference?

I’m a graduate student, and my lab is being audited by the university for equipment usage. A few of us used a department-owned camera for a student film project over a weekend, which technically wasn’t allowed, though nothing was damaged and we returned it on time. The audit form asks whether lab equipment was used only for approved research or teaching purposes. If I mention the film project, my lab might lose checkout privileges for everyone. My lab mates want me to leave it out since it was harmless. What should I do?

I manage scheduling at a café, and our district manager is reviewing payroll because labor costs are high. Last month, I let several employees stay clocked in while business was slow so they could make rent, even though the company policy says to cut shifts early when sales drop. Now I’m supposed to explain the excess hours. I could say a delivery issue kept us understaffed and busy, which would protect my staff and probably avoid write-ups. If I tell the full story, people may lose hours going forward. How should I handle it?

I’m organizing travel reimbursement for a nonprofit conference. Several volunteers shared hotel rooms to save money, but one person lost a receipt for a rideshare from the airport. The finance office requires receipts for every reimbursement, and they’re strict. Another volunteer suggested we submit a screenshot from a different ride with a similar amount, since the missing expense was real and the reimbursement would help cover costs for people who paid out of pocket. I’m the person sending the packet to the institution. Should I include the substitute screenshot or explain the missing receipt?
